In front of the vault is a tray with two bays, pending and claimable. Step {step1}: the investor calls {requestFn}, and the request waits in the pending bay; {pendingFn} returns {amount}. Step {step2}: the vault processes and prices the request, which moves to the claimable bay; {claimableFn} returns {amount} and {pendingFn} zero. Step {step3}: the investor claims with {claimFn} and receives {received}; both view functions return zero for the request. A vault can make a request claimable right away, but the claim is always a separate call.
token-vault-lifecycle-step-idle: Choose a deposit or a redemption and send the request to follow it through its three states.
token-vault-lifecycle-step-request: Step {step}: pending. The investor has called {requestFn}, and the vault holds {amount} for the request: {pendingFn} returns {amount}.
token-vault-lifecycle-step-fulfill: Step {step}: claimable. The vault has processed and priced the request: {claimableFn} returns {amount}, and {pendingFn} zero. The standard defines no event for the change.
token-vault-lifecycle-step-claim: Step {step}: claimed. The investor calls {claimFn} and receives {received}; both view functions return zero for this request.
merkle-proof-title: Checking a value with a Merkle proof
merkle-proof-caption: A Merkle proof is one hash per level of the tree. Combined with the value, level by level, it must give back the root stored onchain.
merkle-proof-description: A binary Merkle tree drawn top to bottom. At the top is the root, H(A-H), and beside it merkleRoot, the copy of the root stored onchain. Below are two hashes, H(A-D) and H(E-H), then four, H(A-B) to H(G-H), and at the bottom the {leaves} values A to H, the first {leaves} entries of the article's dataArray. Each hash is the pairHash of the two nodes below it. With C chosen, step {step1}: the verifier gets the value C and its proof, D, H(A-B) and H(E-H). Step {step2}: C and D are combined into H(C-D). Step {step3}: H(C-D) and H(A-B) give H(A-D). Step {step4}: H(A-D) and H(E-H) give a computed root, after {proofSize} proof hashes for {leaves} values. Step {step5}: the computed root equals the stored root, so the proof is valid. Proving F uses E, H(G-H) and H(A-D) instead. With a changed C, the same proof gives a different root, and the check fails.
merkle-proof-definition-value: The value to prove, one of the {leaves} leaves. Only it and the proof are sent; the rest of the data stays offchain.
merkle-proof-definition-proof: The hashes to combine with the value, one per level: {proofSize} for {leaves} values. Each level halves the tree, so {bigLeaves} values would need only {bigProofSize}.
merkle-proof-definition-path: The hashes the verifier computes itself: the pairHash of the value, or of the last result, with the next proof hash, up to a candidate root.
merkle-proof-definition-root: The Merkle root, the only part stored onchain (merkleRoot in the contract). The proof is valid only if the computed root equals it.
merkle-proof-step-idle: Choose a value and check the proof to rebuild the root from the value and its proof, then compare it with the stored root.
merkle-proof-step-value: Step {step}: the verifier gets the value {leaf} and its proof: {proof0}, {proof1} and {proof2}. The root is already stored onchain.
merkle-proof-step-tampered-value: Step {step}: the verifier gets {leaf}, a changed copy of C, with C's genuine proof: {proof0}, {proof1} and {proof2}.
merkle-proof-step-level1: Step {step}: pairHash combines {leaf} with its sibling {proof0} into {node1}.
merkle-proof-step-level2: Step {step}: the result is combined with the next proof hash, {proof1}, into {node2}.
merkle-proof-step-level3: Step {step}: combining with {proof2} gives a candidate root. That took {proofSize} hashes for {leaves} values; {bigLeaves} values would need {bigProofSize}.
merkle-proof-step-compare: Step {step}: the computed root equals the stored root, so {leaf} is part of the data.
merkle-proof-step-tampered-compare: Step {step}: the computed root differs from the stored root, so the proof fails and the changed value is rejected.
optimistic-rollup-caption: An optimistic rollup batch: the sequencer posts its data and a new state root to L1, and the root becomes final only if no one proves it wrong before the challenge window ends.
optimistic-rollup-description: Two plates: layer 2 at the back left and Ethereum (L1) in front of it on the right. On layer 2, a stack of transactions feeds the sequencer. A pipe runs from the sequencer to the rollup contracts on L1, which hold the batch data and the state root on top. Beside the contracts stand the operator's bond, a tank of value, and an L1 account that withdrawals go to. A challenger stands at L1's front right, piped to the contracts, and the challenge window runs along L1's front edge as {days} day cells, from day 0 to day {days}. Step {step1}: the sequencer orders and executes the transactions and computes a new state root. Step {step2}: it posts the batch data and the state root to the contracts, staking its bond behind the root. In the honest batch scenario, step {step3}: a challenger re-executes the batch from the data on L1, gets the same root and stays quiet; step {step4}: the {days} days pass with no challenge; step {step5}: the root is final and withdrawals can complete. In the invalid state root scenario, step {step3}: on day {challengeDay} the challenger gets a different root and disputes it, putting a trace of {steps} execution steps in question; step {step4}: bisection halves the disputed steps over {rounds} rounds until one is left; step {step5}: L1 re-executes that one step, the state root is deleted and the bond is slashed, part of it paid to the challenger.
optimistic-rollup-step-idle: Choose a scenario and post the batch to follow it from the sequencer to L1.
optimistic-rollup-step-execute: Step {step}: The sequencer orders the L2 transactions, executes them, and computes the rollup's new state root.
optimistic-rollup-step-post: Step {step}: The sequencer posts the batch data and the new state root to the rollup contracts on L1, staking its bond behind the root. L1 accepts the root without checking it.
optimistic-rollup-step-check: Step {step}: The challenge window opens. A challenger re-executes the batch from the data on L1, gets the same state root, and doesn't dispute it.
optimistic-rollup-step-elapse: Step {step}: All {days} days of the challenge window pass with no challenge.
optimistic-rollup-step-finalize: Step {step}: The state root is final. Withdrawals in the batch can now complete on L1, and the operator can take back its bond.
optimistic-rollup-step-challenge: Step {step}: On day {challengeDay}, a challenger re-executes the batch, gets a different state root, and disputes it. All {steps} steps of the batch's execution are in question.
optimistic-rollup-step-bisect: Step {step}: Bisection. The operator splits the disputed steps into two halves and the challenger picks the half it disagrees with, for {rounds} rounds, until a single step is left.
optimistic-rollup-step-prove: Step {step}: L1 re-executes that one step and finds the operator's result wrong. The state root is deleted and the operator's bond is slashed. In designs like this one, part goes to the challenger and the rest is burned.
optimistic-rollup-status-post: Batch and state root posted to L1
optimistic-rollup-status-finalize: State root final: withdrawals can complete
optimistic-rollup-status-prove: One-step proof: root deleted, bond slashed
optimistic-rollup-definition-txs: Transactions users send to the rollup, executed off Ethereum.
optimistic-rollup-definition-sequencer: The rollup's operator: it orders and executes L2 transactions and posts batches and state roots to L1, backed by a bond. Some rollups have a separate proposer post the state roots.
optimistic-rollup-definition-batch: The batch's compressed transaction data, posted to L1 as calldata or in blobs, so anyone can re-execute it.
optimistic-rollup-definition-contracts: The rollup's smart contracts on Ethereum: they store state roots, hold deposits and bonds, and settle disputes.
optimistic-rollup-definition-state-root: The Merkle root of the rollup's state after the batch. L1 accepts it optimistically and deletes it if a fraud proof shows it is wrong.
optimistic-rollup-definition-bond: Value the operator stakes behind its state root, slashed if the root is proven invalid.
optimistic-rollup-definition-window: The challenge period, during which anyone can dispute the state root: about {days} days on the major rollups, though each rollup sets its own.
optimistic-rollup-definition-challenger: Any node that re-executes the batch from the data on L1 and disputes a state root it disagrees with.
optimistic-rollup-definition-trace: The batch's execution, step by step: {steps} steps here, billions in a real batch, which takes more bisection rounds.
optimistic-rollup-definition-account: An address on Ethereum that receives a withdrawal from the rollup once the state root is final.
optimistic-rollup-definition-l2: The rollup chain, where transactions execute off Ethereum.
optimistic-rollup-definition-l1: Ethereum Mainnet, the layer 1 that stores the rollup's data and settles its disputes.
base-fee-caption: Each block's base fee follows from the gas used in the block before it: above the target it rises, below it falls, by at most {max} per block. The base fee is burned.
base-fee-description: A chart of {blocks} consecutive blocks and the next one. In the lower half, a bar for each block shows the gas it used, against the gas limit of {limit} gas and a dashed target line at half of it, {target} gas. In the upper half, a line of steps shows each block's base fee in gwei, starting at {start} gwei ({coolingStart} gwei in the cooling off scenario). A block's base fee is set by the block before it: if that block used more gas than the target, the base fee rises, and if it used less, the base fee falls, in proportion to the gap and by at most {max}. A full block raises it by {max}, an empty block lowers it by {max}, and a block exactly on target leaves it unchanged. The base fee is burned, so each block removes its gas used times its base fee from circulation, while the priority fee goes to the validator. In the demand spike scenario the first block is three-quarters full and every block after it is full and the base fee climbs {max} per block; in cooling off, empty and then lightly used blocks make it fall; on target keeps it flat. You can change a block's gas used by dragging its bar or with the controls, and the base fees after it are worked out again. Building the blocks adds them one at a time, each followed by the base fee it sets for the next block.
base-fee-step-idle: Choose a scenario or drag a block's bar to change its gas used, then build the blocks to watch the base fee adjust.
base-fee-step-up: Step {step}: block {block} uses {used} gas, {percent} of its target, so the base fee rises {change} to {next} gwei for block {nextBlock}.
base-fee-step-down: Step {step}: block {block} uses {used} gas, {percent} of its target, so the base fee falls {change} to {next} gwei for block {nextBlock}.
base-fee-step-flat: Step {step}: block {block} uses exactly its target of {used} gas, so block {nextBlock} keeps the base fee of {next} gwei.
base-fee-status-up: Block {block}: {percent} of target, base fee up {change}
base-fee-status-down: Block {block}: {percent} of target, base fee down {change}
base-fee-status-flat: Block {block}: on target, base fee unchanged
base-fee-definition-base-fee: The minimum price per unit of gas in a block, set by the protocol from the block before. It is burned.
base-fee-definition-limit: The most gas a block can use: twice the target.
base-fee-definition-target: Half the gas limit. A block above it raises the next base fee; a block below it lowers it.
base-fee-definition-block: The gas a block's transactions used. Drag a bar to change it.
gasper-finality-caption: Casper FFG, one epoch at a time: the votes cast during an epoch target its checkpoint. If they reach two-thirds of the stake by the end of the epoch, the supermajority link justifies that checkpoint and finalizes the one before it. With less, finality stalls.
gasper-finality-description: A timeline of epochs {first} to {last}, left to right, with their names under the checkpoints. Each epoch is {slots} slots of {seconds} seconds: it starts with its checkpoint, a large block, followed by its other blocks, up to a dashed boundary where the next epoch starts. Under each epoch from the second on, a bar spans the whole epoch and fills as its slots pass, showing the share of all staked ETH whose validators have attested so far, with a tick at two-thirds. An arrow from the bar up to the epoch's checkpoint shows that every vote cast during the epoch names that checkpoint as its target, and the last justified checkpoint as its source. Checkpoint {first} starts justified, and {earlier} is already finalized. Each step plays one epoch. At its end boundary the votes are counted: when they reach at least two-thirds, the link from source to target is a supermajority link, drawn as an arch between the two checkpoints. The epoch's checkpoint is justified, and the justified checkpoint before it is finalized and shown with a lock. In the healthy and just-enough scenarios this repeats every epoch, so each checkpoint is finalized about two epochs after it is proposed. In the too-few scenario every bar stops short of the tick, the new checkpoints stay unjustified, nothing more is finalized, and if that lasts more than {leak} epochs the inactivity leak starts.
gasper-finality-step-idle: Choose a scenario and run the epochs to watch checkpoints get justified and finalized. Each epoch is {slots} slots of {seconds} seconds and starts with its checkpoint. Validators attest throughout the epoch, and the votes are counted at its end. Checkpoint {first} is already justified.
gasper-finality-step-justify-first: Step {step}: through epoch {epoch}, validators attest with checkpoint {epoch} as their target and {source} as their source. At the end of the epoch, {share} of the staked ETH has attested, at least two-thirds: the supermajority link justifies {epoch} and finalizes {source}.
gasper-finality-step-justify-next: Step {step}: through epoch {epoch}, the votes target checkpoint {epoch}, with {source} as their source. At the end of the epoch they reach {share} of the staked ETH, so {epoch} is justified and {source} is finalized, about two epochs after it was proposed.
gasper-finality-step-justify-last: Step {step}: through epoch {epoch}, the votes target {epoch}, with {source} as their source. At the end of the epoch they reach {share}, so {epoch} is justified and {source} is finalized. While at least two-thirds of the stake attests, every epoch's end justifies its checkpoint and finalizes the one before it.
gasper-finality-step-stall-first: Step {step}: through epoch {epoch}, validators attest with checkpoint {epoch} as their target and {source} as their source. At the end of the epoch only {share} of the staked ETH has attested, less than two-thirds: there is no supermajority link, so {epoch} stays unjustified.
gasper-finality-step-stall-next: Step {step}: through epoch {epoch}, the votes target {epoch}, with {source}, still the last justified checkpoint, as their source. At the end of the epoch they reach only {share}: {epoch} stays unjustified and nothing new is finalized.
gasper-finality-step-stall-last: Step {step}: epoch {epoch} also ends with only {share}, short of two-thirds, so nothing has been finalized since {finalized}. If the chain fails to finalize for more than {leak} epochs, the inactivity leak starts draining the stake of validators who are not attesting.
gasper-finality-status-stall: End of {epoch}: short of two-thirds, finality stalls
gasper-finality-definition-link: Votes from at least two-thirds of the staked ETH linking the last justified checkpoint (the source) to the current epoch's checkpoint (the target).
gasper-finality-definition-meter: The share of all staked ETH whose validators attested during this epoch. Every vote names the epoch's checkpoint as its target.
gasper-finality-definition-threshold: The supermajority: two-thirds of the total staked ETH. A link needs at least this much by the end of the epoch.
gasper-finality-definition-boundary: Where the epoch ends and the next begins. Its votes are counted here, and checkpoints are justified and finalized.
gasper-finality-definition-justified: A checkpoint that a supermajority link points to. Unlikely to be reverted, but it can be.
gasper-finality-definition-finalized: A justified checkpoint with a justified checkpoint right after it. Reverting it would mean destroying at least a third of the staked ETH.
gasper-finality-definition-proposed: An epoch's checkpoint without a supermajority link to it yet.
gasper-finality-definition-blocks: The epoch's other blocks. An epoch is {slots} slots of {seconds} seconds, and only its first block is a checkpoint.
gasper-finality-definition-upcoming: An epoch that has not started yet.
zk-rollup-caption: A ZK-rollup batch: the operator posts its data, a new state root and a validity proof to L1, and the root is recorded, and final, only if the verifier contract accepts the proof. There is no challenge window.
zk-rollup-description: Two plates: layer 2 at the back left and Ethereum (L1) in front of it on the right. On layer 2, a stack of transactions feeds the sequencer, and a prover stands in front of the sequencer. A pipe runs from the sequencer to the rollup contract on L1, which holds the batch data and the state root on top. A second pipe runs from the prover to the verifier contract, which stands in front of the rollup contract and is piped to it. Beside them stands an L1 account that withdrawals go to. Step {step1}: the sequencer orders and executes the transactions and computes a new state root. Step {step2}: the prover generates a validity proof for the batch. Step {step3}: the operator posts the batch data, the new state root and the proof to L1. In the valid batch scenario, step {step4}: the verifier contract checks the proof and accepts it; step {step5}: the rollup contract records the new state root, which is final at once, and withdrawals can complete. In the invalid state transition scenario, the sequencer computes a wrong state root in step {step1}, and in step {step2} no valid proof can be produced for it; step {step4}: the verifier contract rejects the proof posted with it; step {step5}: the call reverts, the wrong state root is never recorded and withdrawals in the batch can't complete.
zk-rollup-step-idle: Choose a scenario and post the batch to follow it from the sequencer to L1.
zk-rollup-step-execute: Step {step}: The sequencer orders the L2 transactions, executes them, and computes the rollup's new state root.
zk-rollup-step-prove: Step {step}: The prover generates a validity proof, a ZK-SNARK or ZK-STARK, that executing the batch turns the old state root into the new one. Proving takes heavy computation, so it can be slow and costly.
zk-rollup-step-post: Step {step}: The operator posts the batch data (as calldata or in blobs), the new state root and the proof to the rollup's contracts on L1.
zk-rollup-step-verify: Step {step}: The verifier contract checks the proof against the old state root, the new one and the batch, without re-executing the transactions. The proof is valid.
zk-rollup-step-finalize: Step {step}: The rollup contract records the new state root. It is final as soon as the proof is verified, with no challenge window, so withdrawals in the batch can complete on L1.
zk-rollup-step-execute-bad: Step {step}: The sequencer executes the L2 transactions but computes a wrong new state root, through a bug or on purpose.
zk-rollup-step-prove-bad: Step {step}: No valid proof exists for a wrong state transition, so the prover can't produce one. Any proof the operator submits for this root will fail.
zk-rollup-step-post-bad: Step {step}: The operator posts the batch data, the wrong state root and an invalid proof to the rollup's contracts on L1.
zk-rollup-step-reject: Step {step}: The verifier contract checks the proof against the old state root, the new one and the batch, and rejects it.
zk-rollup-step-revert: Step {step}: The call reverts. The wrong state root is never recorded, the rollup's state on L1 stays at the last verified root, and withdrawals in the batch can't complete.
zk-rollup-status-post: Batch, state root and proof posted to L1
zk-rollup-status-finalize: State root recorded and final: withdrawals can complete
zk-rollup-status-prove-bad: No valid proof can be produced
zk-rollup-status-post-bad: Batch, wrong state root and invalid proof posted
zk-rollup-definition-txs: Transactions users send to the rollup, executed off Ethereum.
zk-rollup-definition-sequencer: The rollup's operator: it orders and executes L2 transactions, builds batches and posts them to L1. Some ZK-rollups rotate this role among staked operators.
zk-rollup-definition-prover: Generates the validity proof for a batch. Proving takes heavy computation, so it can be slow and costly, and it often runs separately from the sequencer.
zk-rollup-definition-proof: A succinct proof, a ZK-SNARK or ZK-STARK, that executing the batch turns the old state root into the new one. Ethereum checks it without re-executing the transactions.
zk-rollup-definition-batch: The batch's compressed transaction data or state differences, posted to L1 as calldata or in blobs, so anyone can reconstruct the rollup's state.
zk-rollup-definition-contracts: The rollup's main contract on Ethereum: it stores batches and state roots, holds deposits and processes withdrawals.
zk-rollup-definition-state-root: The Merkle root of the rollup's state after the batch. The rollup contract records it only if the batch's validity proof verifies.
zk-rollup-definition-verifier: A contract on Ethereum that checks validity proofs against the old state root, the new one and the batch. Verifying costs gas, but far less than re-executing the batch.
zk-rollup-definition-account: An address on Ethereum that receives a withdrawal from the rollup once the batch's proof is verified. The wait is for proving, not a challenge window, though some rollups add a delay of their own.
zk-rollup-definition-l2: The rollup chain, where transactions execute off Ethereum.
zk-rollup-definition-l1: Ethereum Mainnet, the layer 1 that stores the rollup's data and verifies its proofs.
